predictions.explanation:
Evidence from 2023–early 2025 shows a broad, time‑bounded distress period for startups that raised at peak 2020–2021 valuations and later struggled on revenue growth or burn, matching the normalized prediction.

* **Down rounds became unusually common, especially 2023–Q1 2024.** Carta’s State of Private Markets reports show that in 2023 roughly 19–20% of all US venture rounds were down rounds every quarter—the highest rates since at least 2018, leading Carta and multiple analysts to dub 2023 “the year of the down round.”([carta.com](https://carta.com/data/state-of-private-markets-q4-2023/?utm_source=openai)) In Q1 2024, down rounds climbed further to about 23–24% of all deals, a five‑year high.([linkedin.com](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/carta--_state-of-private-markets-q1-2024-report-snapshot-activity-7193645427915649025-X5mw?utm_source=openai)) That is roughly double the pre‑2022 norm of ~10%.([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/kylewestaway/2025/02/24/the-new-venture-playbook-the-data-every-founder-needs-to-know/?utm_source=openai))
* **Bridge rounds and stalled progression (i.e., inability to raise “well”) spiked.** Carta data shows that in 2023–2024 around 40% of seed and Series A financings were bridge rounds rather than clean new priced rounds, reflecting companies that could not secure traditional up‑rounds.([carta.com](https://carta.com/data/state-of-private-markets-q4-2023/?utm_source=openai)) Axios, citing Carta, notes that by Q1 2024, 46% of seed deals were bridges and that Series A activity had plunged 79% versus 2022, indicating severe difficulty raising new institutional capital on favorable terms.([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/newsletters/axios-pro-rata-a68c1560-d690-4439-b7d7-8e1e4d8e8c2b?utm_source=openai))
* **Most seed‑stage companies from the 2020–2022 boom could not raise a proper Series A.** Multiple analyses of Carta data show that only about 15% of companies that raised seed in early 2022 managed to raise a Series A within two years—roughly half the historical graduation rate (~30%).([konvoy.vc](https://www.konvoy.vc/newsletters/failure-to-launch-the-series-a-crunch?utm_source=openai)) That implies that *most* of that cohort either failed outright, remained stuck on extensions/bridges (effective restructurings), or raised at unattractive terms if they raised at all.
* **Explicit link to 2020–2021 “peak valuation” cohorts running out of runway.** A 2023 venture deal‑points study notes that down rounds in 2023 were 2.25× the average of 2020–2022, and explains this by saying that companies which raised at very high pandemic‑era valuations had exhausted their cash runways and prior bridge strategies and were “forced to go back to the market in 2023, where valuations were markedly lower.”([mondaq.com](https://www.mondaq.com/canada/corporate-and-company-law/1453432/2023-deal-points-report-venture-capital-financings?utm_source=openai)) That is precisely the scenario the prediction describes: 2020–2021 vintage companies, now out of money and underperforming, facing down rounds or equivalent.
* **Restructurings and shutdowns surged in the same 1–2 year window.** Carta‑based analyses show startup shutdowns rose 58% between Q1 2023 and Q1 2024 as funding tightened, with capital increasingly concentrated in a small set of favored areas (notably AI).([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2024/08/20/startup-closures-rising-2024-economy?utm_source=openai)) Separate Carta data reported by the Wall Street Journal show that 2023 was the first year in at least five years in which startup headcount *shrank* in aggregate, driven by layoffs and hiring freezes as companies restructured to conserve cash amid tight capital markets.([wsj.com](https://www.wsj.com/articles/startup-head-count-shrank-for-the-first-time-in-years-carta-says-69384f56?utm_source=openai))
* **The stress period was indeed about 1–2 years and then began to ease.** By mid‑2024, Carta’s Q2 2024 report notes that down‑round rates fell from ~24% in Q1 to ~17% and suggests that, as the 2020–2021 high‑valuation vintages work through the system, the incidence of such harsh repricings should decline.([carta.com](https://carta.com/data/state-of-private-markets-q2-2024/?utm_source=openai)) This supports the idea of a discrete 2023–early‑2024 distress window rather than an indefinite new normal.

Taken together, the data shows that from roughly early 2023 through early/mid‑2024 there was a broad, historically severe funding squeeze in which:

* Down rounds and punitive terms were at multi‑year highs;
* Bridge rounds and extensions were ubiquitous at seed and Series A;
* The majority of seed‑stage companies from the 2020–2022 boom could not progress to normal new rounds; and
* Shutdowns, layoffs, and restructurings spiked.

This lines up with the normalized claim that *most* underperforming 2020–2021‑vintage startups running out of money would face down rounds, restructurings, or an inability to raise on acceptable terms over a 1–2 year period starting around Q1 2023. While we lack a perfect census of every such company, the scale and timing of the documented distress strongly support judging the prediction as broadly correct rather than inconclusive or wrong.

predictions.explanation:
**Assessment window**: The prediction was about the ~1–2 years after the 2020–2021 valuation bubble (i.e., roughly 2023–early 2025). We now have data through late 2025.

**1. Distress for 2020–2021 “bubble” companies**  
Multiple datasets show sustained stress for companies that raised at peak valuations:

- 2023 VC funding fell sharply; about 20% of rounds were down rounds, the highest share since the GFC, with prominent late‑stage failures and bankruptcies (WeWork, Convoy, Bird, etc.). Late‑stage valuations were at multi‑year lows and unicorn blow‑ups were common. ([mbmcapital.co](https://www.mbmcapital.co/insights/2023-annual-report?utm_source=openai))  
- Analysis of the post‑“everything bubble” environment projected hundreds of unicorns (many minted 2019–2022) losing their status, and noted that a large subset of these 2020–2021 mega‑round companies had <6 months of runway by 2023, implying acute funding stress. ([equiam.com](https://equiam.com/insights/shifting-tides-2023?utm_source=openai))  
- Carta data show down‑round rates roughly doubled to ~20% over the last two years vs ~10% in 2019–mid‑2022, with 2022–2023 described as the period when middle‑ and late‑stage companies “felt the sharpest pains,” followed only in 2024 by the *beginnings* of a recovery. ([edwardconard.com](https://www.edwardconard.com/macro-roundup/cartainc-finds-venture-valuations-have-undergone-a-reset-in-the-last-two-years-with-the-rate-of-down-rounds-running-20-in-the-last-two-years-up-from-10-between-2019-and-mid-20/?view=detail&utm_source=openai))  
- As of 2025, down rounds remain elevated (about 15.9% of deals), indicating that distress for many bubble‑era companies persisted into the predicted window. ([coinlaw.io](https://coinlaw.io/venture-capital-industry-statistics/?utm_source=openai))  

Taken together, this matches a broad 1–2 year period of material distress for the 2020–2021 cohort.

**2. Relative resurgence for new/early‑stage startups**  
At the same time, conditions for *new* companies—especially at pre‑seed/seed—were comparatively favorable:

- 2023 was “a tale of two markets”: seed and pre‑seed remained robust, with deal sizes and valuations at 10‑year highs, even as later‑stage activity cratered. ([mbmcapital.co](https://www.mbmcapital.co/insights/2023-annual-report?utm_source=openai))  
- PitchBook/Carta data show pre‑seed rounds up 51% in 2023 and growing as a share of seed‑stage deals, indicating strong appetite for very early‑stage startups despite an overall funding pullback. ([vccafe.com](https://www.vccafe.com/2024/02/27/how-the-pre-seed-round-made-a-comeback-in-2024/?utm_source=openai))  
- By 2024, Carta reports seed valuations hitting record highs and intense competition for the most attractive early‑stage deals, while 2022–2023 pain remained concentrated in later stages. ([carta.com](https://carta.com/data/state-of-private-markets-q4-2024/?utm_source=openai))  
- Angel investor data show pre‑seed and seed valuations surging in 2024, even as Series B+ valuations fell sharply—another sign that capital was relatively more welcoming to new companies than to bubble‑era growth firms. ([angelcapitalassociation.org](https://angelcapitalassociation.org/blog/the-early-stage-valuation-disconnect/?utm_source=openai))  

There is nuance: some reports note that *volume* of early‑stage deals hit lows in 2024, even as valuations and competition for the best newcos rose. ([kingsoncapital.com](https://kingsoncapital.com/2025/04/22/vc-trends-2024-year-in-review/?utm_source=openai))  But Gurley’s phrasing—“a little bit of a resurgence for new companies”—is directionally consistent with the data on pre‑seed/seed robustness and investor interest.

**Conclusion**: The core dynamics he described—a 1–2 year stretch of distress for 2020–2021 bubble companies alongside a relative resurgence in opportunity for newly founded startups—materialized broadly as predicted.

predictions.explanation:
Available data show that **only a minority of the 2021 unicorn cohort has actually raised down rounds so far**, and most have not tested a new priced valuation since the peak – but the prediction is about what will happen *eventually*, so it can’t be definitively verified or falsified yet.

Key evidence:
- Carta data on 616 U.S. unicorns valued at ≥$1B as of December 31, 2021 show that by 2024: 14 had shut down, 78 had exited (IPO or M&A), and 524 remained. Only 150 of those 524 (29%) raised *any* financing after the start of 2022, and just 67 (about 13% of the total cohort) raised a **down round**. Among the unicorns that *did* raise, down rounds were 45% of primary rounds, but that’s still far from “nearly 100%” of all unicorns. ([linkedin.com](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/peterjameswalker_startups-unicorns-founders-activity-7296952370142265345-XRY2))
- A Bloomberg analysis using Carta data on 354 companies that first became unicorns in 2021 similarly finds that **fewer than 30%** have raised financing in the three years since; among those that did, “almost half” were down rounds. This again implies that only on the order of ~15% of the cohort has actually done a down round so far. ([edwardconard.com](https://www.edwardconard.com/macro-roundup/katie_roof-describes-the-era-of-the-zombie-unicorn-noting-that-of-354-vc-backed-firms-valued-over-1b-in-2021-only-10-went-public-via-ipos-or-spacs-many-are-now-facing/?view=detail))
- These figures are consistent with broader research on the “global unicorn club,” which notes that there are still 1,200+ active unicorns worldwide and that many 2021‑era unicorns remain private and have not repriced via a new round or IPO yet. ([cbinsights.com](https://www.cbinsights.com/research/global-tech-unicorn-peak-q3-2023/?utm_source=openai))
- There are also prominent **counterexamples to an across‑the‑board down‑round dynamic** among 2021‑era unicorns. For example, OpenAI, already a unicorn before 2022, has raised successive *up* rounds, culminating in a $40B round at a $300B valuation in 2025—nearly double its prior $157B valuation—rather than a down round. ([coincodex.com](https://coincodex.com/article/33434/openai-valuation/?utm_source=openai))  This suggests at least some members of the 2021 unicorn set can continue raising at higher valuations.

However, Brad Gerstner’s claim was explicitly that **“100%” of roughly 1,000 end‑of‑2021 unicorns will *eventually* raise capital in a down round before the valuation reset is complete.** Because:
- A large share of that cohort has not yet raised any new primary financing or gone through a definitive end‑state (shutdown, permanent public‑market life without new equity issuance, etc.), and
- The notion of when the “valuation reset” is “complete” is itself vague and debated,

we cannot yet say with confidence what fraction will *ultimately* experience down‑round capital raises. Current evidence strongly contradicts the *spirit* of “100%” so far (we’re nowhere near that today), but it does **not** logically rule out more down rounds in the future for many still‑private unicorns.

Given the open‑ended timeframe and incomplete funding histories, the fairest classification as of November 30, 2025 is **“inconclusive (too early)”**, rather than definitively right or wrong.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence from late 2023–2025 shows that Brad’s prediction largely played out:

1. **IPO window reopened for tech after August 2023**  
   * After an 18‑month tech IPO drought, Arm’s September 2023 listing was the biggest IPO of the year and was explicitly described as a potential *catalyst* for dozens of stuck tech IPO plans, with Instacart and Klaviyo among those filing alongside it. ([fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2023/09/06/arm-holdings-half-ipo-ambitions-487-billion-still-world-biggest-2023-softbank/?utm_source=openai))  
   * Instacart (CART) went public days later at a ~$10B valuation and was widely reported as the first notable U.S. venture‑backed tech IPO since December 2021, marking a reopening of the tech IPO market. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/amp/2023/09/18/instacart-prices-ipo-at-30-a-share.html?utm_source=openai))  
   * In 1Q 2024, Reddit and Astera Labs priced sizable tech IPOs, with Renaissance Capital noting that the U.S. IPO market was rebounding and that 1Q24 signaled the end of a two‑year freeze, as more large names came public and performed well. ([renaissancecapital.com](https://www.renaissancecapital.com/IPO-Center/News/103877/US-IPO-Weekly-Recap-Tech-IPOs-pop-as-end-of-March-approaches?utm_source=openai))  
   * By year‑end 2024, there were about 150 U.S. IPOs raising $29.6B—over 50% more proceeds than 2023—with venture‑backed tech IPOs like Reddit contributing to the recovery, and 2025 commentary describing the IPO market as “rebounding fast.” ([barrons.com](https://www.barrons.com/articles/wall-street-ipo-2024-renaissance-capital-2791b5b6?utm_source=openai))  
   This supports the idea that, starting in the near term after August 2023, a new wave of IPOs—especially in tech—did materialize, even if volumes remained below 2021’s peak.

2. **Presence of ‘first‑class’ / high‑quality tech IPOs**  
   Multiple large, well‑known, or strongly performing tech offerings appeared in this period, consistent with “first class IPOs”:
   * **Arm** – a globally important chip designer, largest IPO of 2023, with a ~$54–55B valuation and strong first‑day trading; seen as a crucial test for and catalyst to the broader tech IPO market. ([fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2023/09/13/arm-ipo-valuation-stock-price-nasdaq/?utm_source=openai))  
   * **Reddit** and **Astera Labs** – high‑profile, substantial tech listings in March 2024; Astera popped ~70%+ on day one, and Reddit raised ~$748M, later cited by Renaissance as part of a strong cohort of large growth IPOs. ([renaissancecapital.com](https://www.renaissancecapital.com/IPO-Center/News/103877/US-IPO-Weekly-Recap-Tech-IPOs-pop-as-end-of-March-approaches?utm_source=openai))  
   * **Ibotta** and **Rubrik** – further tech IPOs in April 2024; Fortune and TechCrunch framed Ibotta as the third major U.S. tech IPO of 2024 after Reddit and Astera, noting “warming public‑market interest in tech shares” and that tech IPOs were “rolling” again. ([fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2024/04/18/ibotta-shares-surge-ipo-reddit-astera-rubrik/?utm_source=openai))  
   Together these show a stream of significant, high‑quality tech IPOs, not just one‑offs.

3. **Wave of ‘down‑round’ IPOs (public at lower valuations than last private rounds)**  
   Brad also predicted many IPOs would come at valuations below their peak private marks, which clearly occurred:
   * **Instacart** – IPO valued the company around $9.9–10B, down dramatically from its $39B private valuation in 2021 (a ~75% cut). ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/amp/2023/09/18/instacart-prices-ipo-at-30-a-share.html?utm_source=openai))  
   * **Klaviyo** – targeted an ~$8.3B IPO valuation versus a $9.5B private valuation in 2021, a notable step down. ([fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2023/09/15/arm-ipo-strategy-valuation/?utm_source=openai))  
   * **Reddit** – went public at about a $6.4B valuation after having been valued at over $10B in a 2021 funding round, roughly a one‑third markdown. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit?utm_source=openai))  
   * **ServiceTitan** – its 2024 IPO valued it at roughly $9B, slightly below a prior $9.5B valuation from a 2021 funding round. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/technology/software-startup-servicetitan-valued-897-bln-shares-jump-42-nasdaq-debut-2024-12-12/?utm_source=openai))  
   * A broader pattern: commentary on recent IPOs notes that Instacart, Reddit, and Klaviyo all priced below their late‑stage private valuations, and that IPOs “can price below last private rounds,” highlighting this as a common outcome for late‑stage tech firms. ([linkedin.com](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/colinlernell_recent-ipo-data-reveals-a-stark-reality-for-activity-7216033279328575489-nk1V?utm_source=openai))  
   * The Wall Street Journal explicitly described the post‑drought IPO market as “stirring, but at down‑round valuations,” with multiple companies preparing offerings at significantly reduced valuations. ([wsj.com](https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-ipo-market-is-stirring-but-at-down-round-valuations-1bbbed1e?utm_source=openai))  
   This aligns closely with the prediction that a notable share of the new IPO cohort would be down‑rounds.

**Synthesis:**  
Within roughly 6–18 months after August 2023, we saw (a) a clear restart of the tech IPO market from a near standstill, (b) several large, high‑quality tech IPOs (Arm, Reddit, Astera Labs, Ibotta, Rubrik, etc.), and (c) a meaningful subset of those and other listings occurring at valuations materially below their last private rounds (Instacart, Reddit, Klaviyo and others), with financial press explicitly characterizing the new activity as a recovery featuring many down‑round IPOs.  

Given this, Brad’s qualitative forecast about *the nature* of the next IPO wave—its timing (near‑term after Aug 2023), the re‑emergence of strong tech IPOs, and the prevalence of down‑round IPOs—has been borne out by subsequent events. Hence the prediction is **right** in substance, even though the overall IPO market has not yet returned to 2021‑style volumes.

predictions.explanation:
**Summary:**
Brad Gerstner’s detailed timing/size forecast for the tech & growth IPO window in late‑2023 and early‑2024 did not come true, even though his broad directional view that the IPO market would be more open by late 2024 was broadly correct.

**1. Q4 2023: “five, six, seven…good size IPOs” in tech & growth**  
Independent data show that the overall Q4 2023 IPO environment was still weak and produced very few large IPOs of any kind, let alone 5–7 sizable tech/growth IPOs:

- On US exchanges, Q4 2023 had **40 IPOs raising only $4.2B total**, with *traditional* IPOs averaging about **$105M** in proceeds. Birkenstock was explicitly noted as **the only IPO in Q4 2023 to raise over $1B**. ([ideagen.com](https://www.ideagen.com/thought-leadership/blog/q4-2023-ipo-trends?utm_source=openai))  
- Globally, EY’s IPO barometer similarly lists just **three largest Q4 2023 IPOs worldwide**—Birkenstock (Germany, ~$1.48B), ADES Holding (Saudi Arabia, ~$1.22B), and Pure Health Holding (UAE, ~$986M)—and describes the quarter as one where conditions deteriorated and IPOs were postponed. ([ey.com](https://www.ey.com/en_ch/newsroom/2023/12/weak-year-on-the-global-markets-for-ipos?utm_source=openai))  

Even using generous definitions of “sizable” (e.g., >$400–500M) and counting all sectors, the data only support **a handful (≈3)** of large Q4 2023 IPOs worldwide, mostly in consumer/energy/healthcare, not 5–7 tech/growth names. There is no evidence of anything close to 5–7 sizable tech & growth IPOs in that quarter. This sub‑prediction is therefore **wrong**.

**2. Q1 2024: “closer to ten” sizable tech & growth IPOs**  
The first quarter of 2024 did see a few high‑profile growth/tech IPOs, but not anywhere near ~10 sizable ones:

- S&P Global reports that in **Q1 2024 the US had only 25 IPOs total**, with proceeds of **$5.67B**; the **10 largest** IPOs accounted for ~83% of proceeds. The biggest US deals were Reddit (~$860M), Astera Labs (~$820M), and American Healthcare REIT (~$773M). ([spglobal.com](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/articles/2024/4/ipo-activity-slowdown-stretches-through-q1-2024-81213559?utm_source=openai))  
- A separate Q1 2024 review of global IPOs notes major offerings such as Galderma (~$4.8B, dermatology), Amer Sports (~$1.37B, sporting goods), Douglas (~$966M, beauty retail), Reddit (~$860M, social media), Astera Labs (~$809M, semis), and BBB Foods (~$668M, food retail), across multiple sectors. ([ipox.com](https://www.ipox.com/ipox/the-ipox-week-727?utm_source=openai))  

Across these sources you can identify only a **small handful** of clearly “sizable” tech/growth IPOs in Q1 2024 (Reddit, Astera Labs, plus a couple of other growth names depending on classification). The quarter is widely described as **still sluggish**, with global IPO volume and proceeds only modestly up and the market “slowdown” persisting. ([spglobal.com](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/articles/2024/4/ipo-activity-slowdown-stretches-through-q1-2024-81213559?utm_source=openai))  
There is no support for anything like **~10 sizable tech/growth IPOs** in Q1 2024, so this sub‑prediction is also **wrong**.

**3. H2 2024: IPO market “will start opening up” vs. early 2023**  
On the broader trend, Gerstner was closer to the mark. Data for 2024 show a materially more active IPO environment—especially in the Americas—compared with early 2023:

- In **Q1 2023**, there were **33 IPOs on US exchanges**, and only **8 raised more than $50M**; the largest US IPO was just over $700M. EY characterizes this period as another **“quiet”** quarter with IPO activity well below historical norms. ([ey.com](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/ipo/q1-2023-ipo-market-trends?utm_source=openai))  
- By **H1 2024**, EY reports that the Americas had **86 IPOs raising $17.8B**, representing **12% more deals and 67% more proceeds year‑over‑year**, with technology the leading sector by capital raised and a surge in PE/VC‑backed IPOs. ([ey.com](https://www.ey.com/en_lt/insights/ipo/trends?utm_source=openai))  
- Follow‑on reports through Q3 2024 describe the Americas and EMEIA as showing **robust recovery**, with PE/VC‑backed IPOs accounting for a large share of global proceeds and multiple large US offerings (e.g., Viking, Lineage, Rubrik, Waystar, UL Solutions, ServiceTitan) across 2024. ([skadden.com](https://www.skadden.com/insights/publications/2024/06/quarterly-insights/us-capital-markets-midyear-report?utm_source=openai))  

Relative to the very subdued early‑2023 baseline, the IPO market in the second half of 2024 was indeed **materially more open and active**, particularly for larger, PE/VC‑backed and tech‑adjacent growth names. So the **directional** part of his call for a more open window by late 2024 was **broadly right**.

**Overall judgment**  
Because the prediction as posed hinges on all three parts, and the **specific, testable numeric forecasts for Q4 2023 and Q1 2024 clearly did not occur**, the overall prediction must be rated **wrong**, even though his high‑level view that the IPO window would be more open by late 2024 turned out to be roughly correct.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence from 2023–2025 shows that software and startups did go through a **prolonged period of distress beyond mid‑2023**, matching the prediction.

- **Funding environment stayed depressed well after 2022–mid‑2023.** Global VC funding in 2023 fell 42% year‑over‑year to about $248B, the lowest since 2017, with Q4 2023 described as the harshest quarter for global VC in six years and U.S. deal volume at a 10‑year low.([cbinsights.com](https://www.cbinsights.com/research/report/venture-trends-2023/?utm_source=openai)) In 2024, total VC dollars ticked up only modestly and were still roughly half of 2021’s peak, while global deal activity fell to its lowest level since 2016, indicating a continued drought for many startups rather than a quick return to boom‑time conditions.([barrons.com](https://www.barrons.com/articles/venture-capital-investments-2024-ai-766c99dc?utm_source=openai)) Carta data further shows structural strain: by Q1 2024, 46% of seed rounds were bridge rounds and Series A activity had plunged 79% from 2022, highlighting how hard it remained for companies to progress up the funding stack.([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/newsletters/axios-pro-rata-a68c1560-d690-4439-b7d7-8e1e4d8e8c2b?utm_source=openai))

- **Valuations and exits remained under heavy pressure.** CB Insights reports that median late‑stage deal sizes in 2023 were more than 50% smaller than in 2021, and 2023 saw just 170 VC‑backed IPOs worldwide—the fewest in a decade—showing a weak exit market and pressured late‑stage valuations.([cbinsights.com](https://www.cbinsights.com/research/report/venture-trends-2023/?utm_source=openai)) Public SaaS valuations, a key benchmark for private software companies, stayed well below 2021 peaks and only began to rebound meaningfully in late 2024; the PVC SaaS Index was around 7–7.7x sales in 2023–2024, slightly below historical averages and far under the boom‑era multiples.([practicalvc.com](https://practicalvc.com/pvc-saas-index-q4-2024-saas-multiples-rebounding/?utm_source=openai)) Commentators on the software IPO market note that 2023 effectively had only one major software IPO and that even by 2025 the IPO pace is still a fraction of 2021, underscoring how long exits remained constrained.([linkedin.com](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/yes-ipo-market-came-back-2025-still-has-long-way-go-jason-m-lemkin-9yb0c?utm_source=openai))

- **Layoffs and startup failures continued well past mid‑2023.** Tech layoffs in 2023 reached roughly 262,700 workers—59% higher than 2022—according to Layoffs.fyi.([startupnews.fyi](https://startupnews.fyi/2024/02/22/a-comprehensive-list-of-2023-2024-tech-layoffs/?utm_source=openai)) The pain did not stop in 2023: by June 25, 2024, trackers recorded 648 separate tech layoff events affecting over 151,000 people, and coverage described the environment as a continuing “bloodbath,” even if somewhat less severe than 2023.([poetsandquantsforundergrads.com](https://poetsandquantsforundergrads.com/first-jobs/the-tech-bloodbath-is-far-from-over/?utm_source=openai)) Carta’s internal data show that U.S. startup headcount **shrank net in 2023** for the first time in years, with more departures than hires and nearly half of departures being layoffs, while equity grants for new hires dropped by more than a third as valuations cooled and down rounds became more common.([wsj.com](https://www.wsj.com/articles/startup-head-count-shrank-for-the-first-time-in-years-carta-says-69384f56?utm_source=openai)) On top of that, U.S. startup failures surged: FT, citing Carta, reports a 60% rise in startup shutdowns year‑on‑year, with 254 venture‑backed clients going bust in Q1 2024 alone and the bankruptcy rate over seven times 2019 levels.([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/2808ad4c-783f-4475-bcda-bddc0299095e?utm_source=openai))

- **Recovery by 2024–2025 was narrow and uneven.** By 2024–2025, AI‑focused companies attracted huge funding and some SaaS names and IPO candidates began to recover, but overall VC activity and exit volumes remained far below 2021. Global VC in 2024 was still dramatically under 2021 in both dollars and deal count, with investment heavily concentrated in a small set of AI winners and many other software/startup segments struggling to raise or exit.([barrons.com](https://www.barrons.com/articles/venture-capital-investments-2024-ai-766c99dc?utm_source=openai))

Taken together, these data show that after the initial “software recession” leading into mid‑2023, the sector **did endure an extended period—through 2023 and well into 2024—of weak funding, compressed valuations, high layoffs, and elevated shutdowns.** That matches the prediction of a continued, multi‑year stretch of distress and pain rather than a quick post‑2022 snap‑back, so the prediction is best judged as **right**.

VC funding surged (Q4 2024 ten-quarter high per KPMG; Q1 2025 $80B per EY; AI startups raising $89B+), valuations rose (Carta: trending up H1 2025; AI doubling/tripling per Fortune), and deal counts held amid AI boom. predictions.explanation:
Evidence from late 2023 shows that the main macro discussion in the U.S. had indeed shifted from *how high and persistent inflation would be* to *how quickly and smoothly it was coming down*—i.e., to disinflation and the possibility of a soft landing.

1. **Macro data: clear disinflation by late 2023.** U.S. CPI inflation peaked at about 9.1% in June 2022 and then fell sharply through 2023; by late 2023 it had roughly halved, with analysts describing this as an overall *disinflation* of the post‑pandemic inflation surge.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932023_inflation_surge?utm_source=openai))  This is the objective backdrop for any narrative shift: the story was no longer about new highs in inflation, but about the pace at which it was coming down.

2. **Media and analyst framing in 2H 2023: soft landing and disinflation.** By October–December 2023, a large share of high‑profile commentary framed the U.S. macro story as one of *disinflation plus resilient growth*:
   * A November 16, 2023 article on the U.S. “soft landing” noted inflation cooling from 9.1% to 3.2%, emphasizing that **disinflation was occurring while job gains and GDP growth remained strong**, and quoting forecasters who now expected a soft landing.([channelchek.com](https://www.channelchek.com/news-channel/us-economy-achieving-soft-landing-as-inflation-cools-without-recession?utm_source=openai))
   * An October 20, 2023 J.P. Morgan Research piece explicitly said “this disinflation has further to run” and highlighted that **disinflation was occurring alongside resilient growth**, making the core question whether the soft‑landing scenario would hold.([jpmorgan.com](https://www.jpmorgan.com/insights/podcast-hub/research-recap/economic-soft-landing?utm_source=openai))
   * A December 2023 UBS macro update described “progress on disinflation” as central to the outlook and spoke of a “global disinflationary regime,” treating the key issue as the *continuation* of disinflation amid a potential soft landing, not runaway inflation.([ubs.com](https://www.ubs.com/us/en/assetmanagement/insights/market-updates/articles/2023-12-macro-monthly.html?utm_source=openai))
   * A December 2023 National Investment Center outlook noted that many prognosticators were now talking about an “immaculate disinflation,” defined as bringing inflation down without recession—again, centering the narrative on the *disinflation process* rather than on high or rising inflation itself.([nic.org](https://www.nic.org/insider/december-2023/?utm_source=openai))

3. **Fed‑related coverage also emphasized ‘gradual disinflation’.** Reporting around the September 2023 FOMC meeting stressed that Fed officials were increasingly optimistic about achieving a *soft landing with gradual disinflation*. Coverage quoted strategists saying policymakers expected to “achieve gradual disinflation without…triggering a meaningful recession,” and highlighted that inflation had already fallen from 9.1% to around 3.7%.([theintelligencer.net](https://www.theintelligencer.net/news/top-headlines/2023/09/fed-keeps-rates-unchanged-signals-hopes-for-soft-landing/?utm_source=openai))  This is typical of late‑2023 articles, where the angle was: *inflation has fallen a lot; can it keep drifting down without a downturn?*

4. **Contrast with the earlier narrative.** In 2022 and early 2023, mainstream outlets and reference summaries described the situation as an "inflation surge" with multi‑decade‑high price growth and central banks scrambling to respond.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932023_inflation_surge?utm_source=openai)) By late 2023, the same kinds of sources talk about that surge in the past tense and focus on the *disinflation* from those peaks and the prospects of a soft landing. That aligns closely with Brad’s claim that we’d be "talking about disinflation" by the end of 2023.

While headlines still used the word *inflation*, the **dominant framing** in late‑2023 macro commentary was: *inflation has fallen a lot; how durable is this disinflation and can we land softly?* Given the data and the tone of major outlets and institutional research at that time, Brad’s prediction that the prevailing narrative would shift from inflation to disinflation by end‑2023 is best judged as **right**.

predictions.explanation:
Chamath tied exceptionally warm sea surface temperatures (SSTs) in the North Atlantic and off Florida to an increased probability of severe tropical storms and hurricanes in the remainder of the 2023 Atlantic season.

Observations back this up:
- NOAA reported that the North Atlantic had record‑warm SSTs and a prolonged marine heatwave beginning in March 2023, conditions that "contributed to a very active 2023 Atlantic hurricane season." ([climate.gov](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/featured-images/more-year-north-atlantic-has-been-running-fever?utm_source=openai))
- The 2023 Atlantic season produced 20 named storms, 7 hurricanes, and 3 major hurricanes, with an Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) of about 146–148. The 1991–2020 averages are ~14 named storms, 7 hurricanes, 3 major hurricanes, and ACE ~123–125. Thus, storm *quantity* and total energy were clearly above average, even though the number of hurricanes and major hurricanes was near the long‑term mean. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season?utm_source=openai))

NOAA and independent analyses characterize 2023 as an above‑normal, very active Atlantic season, explicitly linking that elevated activity to record‑warm SSTs. ([climate.gov](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/featured-images/more-year-north-atlantic-has-been-running-fever?utm_source=openai)) Given that his prediction was about *elevated probability* of severe storms in a season with anomalously warm SSTs (not a specific count), the subsequent above‑normal activity and energy in the 2023 Atlantic hurricane season align with his claim. Therefore, the prediction is best judged as **right**.

predictions.grok_explanation: The 2023 Atlantic hurricane season was above average in activity despite an El Niño event that typically suppresses storms. It produced 20 named storms (vs. avg. 14), 7 hurricanes (avg. 7), 3 major hurricanes (avg. 3: Franklin Cat 4, Idalia Cat 3, Lee Cat 5), and an ACE index of ~146-148 (20% above 1991-2020 norm of ~120). Multiple sources (NOAA, CSU, Wikipedia, TSR) confirm it ranked 4th most active since 1851/1950, with record North Atlantic SSTs fueling the activity as predicted ([Wikipedia 2023 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season), [NOAA summary](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/2023-atlantic-hurricane-season-ranks-4th-for-most-named-storms-in-year), [CSU verification](https://tropical.colostate.edu/Forecast/2023-11-pressrelease.pdf)).
